message.content: {"schema_version":"teaching-unit.v0.4.0","input_manifest_sha256":"e1005994da31e267f5ce7d25a95226c1910bcd2b2f4170edfed7f789a6c76bfa","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-nc-class-c:lineage:79","source_registry_sha256":"e128656a3d00ba5437556728ebd87f5842c83601163739613417fe77cf9f423b","units":[{"unit_id":"sec15-u01","module_id":"sec15-m01","objective_ids":["sec15-u01"],"title":{"text":"Stop and yield signs","fact_ids":["sec15-F01","sec15-F02","sec15-F03"]},"why_how":[{"text":"The handbook says shape and color identify a sign at a glance, and the octagon is used only for stop signs.","fact_ids":["sec15-F01","sec15-F02"]},{"text":"A stop sign always demands a full stop, while a yield sign demands a stop only when cross traffic requires it.","fact_ids":["sec15-R01","sec15-F07"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Sam reaches a yield sign while a car on the cross street is approaching close enough that Sam would interfere with it.","fact_ids":["sec15-F07","sec15-F06"]},"reasoning":{"text":"At a yield sign, whether you must stop depends on cross traffic; if needed to avoid interfering with it, stop and wait until it passes.","fact_ids":["sec15-F07"]},"result":{"text":"Sam stops and waits until the car passes, then continues.","fact_ids":["sec15-F07","sec15-R01"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Many people think a yield sign never requires a stop.","fact_ids":["sec15-R01"]},"correction":{"text":"A yield sign requires slowing and yielding, with a stop when cross traffic requires it.","fact_ids":["sec15-R01","sec15-F06","sec15-F07"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Stop always, yield sometimes.","fact_ids":["sec15-R01"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"Sam is at a yield sign, and cross traffic is close enough that going on would interfere with it. What should Sam do?","fact_ids":["sec15-F07","sec15-R01"]},"answer":{"text":"Stop and wait until the cross traffic passes.","fact_ids":["sec15-F07"]},"rationale":{"text":"A yield sign calls for a stop when needed to avoid interfering with cross traffic.","fact_ids":["sec15-F07","sec15-F06"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec15-u01-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Signs you must obey","fact_ids":["sec15-F01","sec15-F02","sec15-F06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Three types of signs.","fact_ids":["sec15-F01","sec15-F02","sec15-F06"]},{"text":"The stop octagon.","fact_ids":["sec15-F01","sec15-F02","sec15-F06"]},{"text":"The yield triangle.","fact_ids":["sec15-F01","sec15-F02","sec15-F06"]}],"narration":{"text":"This chapter covers traffic signs and pavement markings. It begins with the two signs that most directly control the right of way: the stop sign and the yield sign. In this lesson you will review how shape and color identify a sign, the three types of signs, what the eight-sided octagon means, where a stop sign is placed and what the law requires there, where exactly to stop, what the downward triangle requires, and when a yield sign turns into a stop. Practice questions often test the difference between the stop duty and the yield duty, so keep them separate.","fact_ids":["sec15-F01","sec15-F02","sec15-F06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec15-u01-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Shape, color and the octagon","fact_ids":["sec15-F01","sec15-F02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Shape and color identify signs.","fact_ids":["sec15-F01","sec15-F02"]},{"text":"Regulatory, warning, guide or informational.","fact_ids":["sec15-F01","sec15-F02"]},{"text":"Octagon: stop signs only.","fact_ids":["sec15-F01","sec15-F02"]}],"narration":{"text":"Shape and color let you identify the kind of highway sign at a glance, and signs fall into three types: regulatory, warning and guide or informational. The eight-sided octagon is used only for stop signs, which show white STOP lettering on a red background. So when you see an octagon, you know it is a stop sign even before you can read the word on it. No other sign uses that shape. The rest of this chapter follows the same idea: each shape and each color carries a meaning, and learning those meanings lets you read signs quickly.","fact_ids":["sec15-F01","sec15-F02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec15-u01-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Stopping at a stop sign","fact_ids":["sec15-F03","sec15-F04","sec15-F05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Usually six to fifty feet before.","fact_ids":["sec15-F03","sec15-F04","sec15-F05"]},{"text":"The law requires a full stop.","fact_ids":["sec15-F03","sec15-F04","sec15-F05"]},{"text":"Move only when the way is clear.","fact_ids":["sec15-F03","sec15-F04","sec15-F05"]}],"narration":{"text":"A stop sign is usually placed six to fifty feet before the intersection, and the law requires a full stop there. After stopping at a stop sign, do not move again until you are certain the way is clear. When a sign or signal requires a stop, stop at the marked stop line. With no stop line or crosswalk, stop before entering the intersection at a point where you can see the cross street. So the stop sign itself may be some distance before the intersection, and the place you stop depends on the markings: the stop line first, otherwise where you can see the cross street.","fact_ids":["sec15-F03","sec15-F04","sec15-F05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":43,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec15-u01-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"The yield triangle","fact_ids":["sec15-F06","sec15-F07"]},"lines":[{"text":"Red and white, pointing down.","fact_ids":["sec15-F06","sec15-F07"]},{"text":"Slow down and give the right of way.","fact_ids":["sec15-F06","sec15-F07"]},{"text":"Stop if cross traffic requires it.","fact_ids":["sec15-F06","sec15-F07"]}],"narration":{"text":"The yield sign is a red and white triangle pointing down, and it requires you to slow down and give the right of way. At a yield sign, whether you must stop depends on cross traffic. If needed to avoid interfering with it, stop and wait until it passes. So the yield sign does not demand a stop every time, but it does demand one when cross traffic is there. If the cross street is clear, you slow down and continue. If cross traffic is approaching and you would interfere with it, you stop and wait until it passes before you go on.","fact_ids":["sec15-F06","sec15-F07"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec15-u01-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Stop or yield","fact_ids":["sec15-R01","sec15-R02","sec15-F03","sec15-F07"]},"lines":[{"text":"Stop: always a full stop.","fact_ids":["sec15-R01","sec15-R02","sec15-F03","sec15-F07"]},{"text":"Yield: stop only when cross traffic requires it.","fact_ids":["sec15-R01","sec15-R02","sec15-F03","sec15-F07"]},{"text":"Octagon stops, triangle yields.","fact_ids":["sec15-R01","sec15-R02","sec15-F03","sec15-F07"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. A stop sign always demands a full stop, while a yield sign demands slowing and yielding, with a stop only when cross traffic requires it. Practice questions may suggest a rolling stop at a clear stop sign, or claim that a yield sign never requires stopping. Neither matches the handbook. The shapes help you keep them apart. The octagon belongs to the stop sign alone, while the downward-pointing triangle belongs to the yield sign. When you see the octagon, it is a full stop every time. When you see the triangle, cross traffic decides whether you stop.","fact_ids":["sec15-R01","sec15-R02","sec15-F03","sec15-F07"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec15-u01-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the yield sign","fact_ids":["sec15-F07","sec15-R01","sec15-F06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Sam is at a yield sign.","fact_ids":["sec15-F07","sec15-R01","sec15-F06"]},{"text":"Cross traffic is close.","fact_ids":["sec15-F07","sec15-R01","sec15-F06"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: Sam reaches a yield sign. A car on the cross street is approaching, close enough that if Sam continued, Sam would interfere with it. What should Sam do? Work it out before reading on. Sam should stop and wait until the cross traffic passes. At a yield sign, whether you must stop depends on cross traffic, and if needed to avoid interfering with it, you stop and wait until it passes. The yield sign is a red and white triangle pointing down, and it requires you to slow down and give the right of way, with a stop when needed.","fact_ids":["sec15-F07","sec15-R01","sec15-F06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec15-u01-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Stop and yield recap","fact_ids":["sec15-F01","sec15-F02","sec15-F03","sec15-F04","sec15-F05","sec15-F06","sec15-F07","sec15-R01","sec15-R02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Octagon: always a full stop.","fact_ids":["sec15-F01","sec15-F02","sec15-F03","sec15-F04","sec15-F05","sec15-F06","sec15-F07","sec15-R01","sec15-R02"]},{"text":"Stop at the line, or where you can see.","fact_ids":["sec15-F01","sec15-F02","sec15-F03","sec15-F04","sec15-F05","sec15-F06","sec15-F07","sec15-R01","sec15-R02"]},{"text":"Triangle: yield, stop if needed.","fact_ids":["sec15-F01","sec15-F02","sec15-F03","sec15-F04","sec15-F05","sec15-F06","sec15-F07","sec15-R01","sec15-R02"]}],"narration":{"text":"Let us recap. Shape and color identify signs, which fall into three types: regulatory, warning and guide or informational. The octagon is used only for stop signs, usually placed six to fifty feet before the intersection, and the law requires a full stop there. Do not move again until you are certain the way is clear. Stop at the marked stop line, or with no line or crosswalk, before entering where you can see the cross street. The downward triangle is the yield sign: slow down and give the right of way, and stop if needed to avoid interfering with cross traffic.","fact_ids":["sec15-F01","sec15-F02","sec15-F03","sec15-F04","sec15-F05","sec15-F06","sec15-F07","sec15-R01","sec15-R02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec15-u02","module_id":"sec15-m02","objective_ids":["sec15-u02"],"title":{"text":"Regulatory and warning signs","fact_ids":["sec15-F08","sec15-F09","sec15-F10"]},"why_how":[{"text":"The handbook says rectangular and square regulatory signs show rules, and disobeying them is a traffic violation.","fact_ids":["sec15-F08","sec15-F09"]},{"text":"Warning signs are diamonds, with black on orange set aside for construction or maintenance areas.","fact_ids":["sec15-F11","sec15-F12","sec15-R03"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Drew is driving on a road and sees a diamond sign in black on orange ahead.","fact_ids":["sec15-F12"]},"reasoning":{"text":"A diamond sign in black on orange warns of a construction or maintenance area, so drive with extra care.","fact_ids":["sec15-F12","sec15-R03"]},"result":{"text":"Drew drives with extra care through the work area.","fact_ids":["sec15-F12"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: treating a black-on-orange diamond as just another ordinary warning.","fact_ids":["sec15-R03"]},"correction":{"text":"A diamond in black on yellow is an ordinary warning, while a diamond in black on orange warns of a construction or maintenance area.","fact_ids":["sec15-R03","sec15-F11","sec15-F12"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Yellow warns, orange works.","fact_ids":["sec15-R03"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"Drew sees a diamond-shaped sign in black on orange. What does it warn of, and how should Drew drive?","fact_ids":["sec15-F12","sec15-R03"]},"answer":{"text":"A construction or maintenance area; drive with extra care.","fact_ids":["sec15-F12"]},"rationale":{"text":"Black on orange sets the diamond apart from the ordinary black-on-yellow warning.","fact_ids":["sec15-R03","sec15-F11"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec15-u02-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Rules and warnings","fact_ids":["sec15-F08","sec15-F10","sec15-F11","sec15-F12"]},"lines":[{"text":"Rectangular regulatory signs.","fact_ids":["sec15-F08","sec15-F10","sec15-F11","sec15-F12"]},{"text":"The no-passing pennant.","fact_ids":["sec15-F08","sec15-F10","sec15-F11","sec15-F12"]},{"text":"Diamond warning signs.","fact_ids":["sec15-F08","sec15-F10","sec15-F11","sec15-F12"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson covers regulatory and warning signs other than stop and yield. You will review what rectangular and square regulatory signs show, what a handicap parking sign reserves, what the yellow pennant marks and how it relates to the DO NOT PASS sign, what diamond-shaped signs give, what a black-on-orange diamond means, and where the STOP AHEAD sign is placed. The colors matter as much as the shapes here, because the same diamond shape can carry an ordinary warning or a warning about a work area, depending on whether it is yellow or orange.","fact_ids":["sec15-F08","sec15-F10","sec15-F11","sec15-F12"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec15-u02-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Rectangles and handicap parking","fact_ids":["sec15-F08","sec15-F09"]},"lines":[{"text":"Speed limits and rules like NO U-TURN.","fact_ids":["sec15-F08","sec15-F09"]},{"text":"Disobeying is a traffic violation.","fact_ids":["sec15-F08","sec15-F09"]},{"text":"Handicap spaces need a plate or placard.","fact_ids":["sec15-F08","sec15-F09"]}],"narration":{"text":"Rectangular and square regulatory signs, usually black and white or red and white, show speed limits and rules such as NO U-TURN, and disobeying them is a traffic violation. A handicap parking sign reserves the space for qualifying people who display a handicap license plate or dashboard placard. So the rectangular regulatory sign is not a suggestion. It states a rule, and breaking it is a violation. The handicap parking sign is one such rule: the space it marks is reserved for qualifying people, and a handicap license plate or a dashboard placard shows that a vehicle may use it.","fact_ids":["sec15-F08","sec15-F09"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec15-u02-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Pennants and diamonds","fact_ids":["sec15-F10","sec15-F11","sec15-F13"]},"lines":[{"text":"Yellow pennant on the left: no passing starts.","fact_ids":["sec15-F10","sec15-F11","sec15-F13"]},{"text":"Diamonds: black on yellow warnings.","fact_ids":["sec15-F10","sec15-F11","sec15-F13"]},{"text":"STOP AHEAD before a hidden stop sign.","fact_ids":["sec15-F10","sec15-F11","sec15-F13"]}],"narration":{"text":"The yellow pennant-shaped sign sits on the left side of the road and marks the start of a no-passing zone, reinforcing the rectangular DO NOT PASS sign. Diamond-shaped signs give cautions or warnings and are normally black on yellow. The STOP AHEAD warning sign is placed well before a stop sign whose view is blocked by a curve or other objects. So the pennant and the DO NOT PASS sign work together on a no-passing zone. The diamond family warns you of what is ahead, and STOP AHEAD is one example, warning you of a stop sign you cannot yet see.","fact_ids":["sec15-F10","sec15-F11","sec15-F13"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec15-u02-s4","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Two pairs to separate","fact_ids":["sec15-R04","sec15-R03","sec15-F10","sec15-F12"]},"lines":[{"text":"Pennant marks the start; DO NOT PASS states the rule.","fact_ids":["sec15-R04","sec15-R03","sec15-F10","sec15-F12"]},{"text":"Yellow diamond: ordinary warning.","fact_ids":["sec15-R04","sec15-R03","sec15-F10","sec15-F12"]},{"text":"Orange diamond: work area.","fact_ids":["sec15-R04","sec15-R03","sec15-F10","sec15-F12"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here are two traps. First, the yellow pennant on the left marks where a no-passing zone begins, while the rectangular DO NOT PASS sign states the rule itself. Second, a diamond in black on yellow is an ordinary warning, while a diamond in black on orange warns of a construction or maintenance area. Practice questions may treat the pennant as the end of a no-passing zone, or treat an orange diamond as an ordinary warning. Neither matches the handbook. The pennant marks the start of the zone. An orange diamond means a work area, where you drive with extra care.","fact_ids":["sec15-R04","sec15-R03","sec15-F10","sec15-F12"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec15-u02-s5","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the orange diamond","fact_ids":["sec15-F12","sec15-R03","sec15-F11"]},"lines":[{"text":"A diamond sign ahead.","fact_ids":["sec15-F12","sec15-R03","sec15-F11"]},{"text":"Black on orange.","fact_ids":["sec15-F12","sec15-R03","sec15-F11"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: Drew is driving and sees a diamond-shaped sign ahead in black on orange. What does it warn of, and how should Drew drive? Work it out before reading on. It warns of a construction or maintenance area, so Drew should drive with extra care. A diamond in black on yellow would be an ordinary warning, but black on orange is set aside for construction or maintenance areas. Both are diamonds, since diamond-shaped signs give cautions or warnings, and the orange color is what tells Drew that the warning is about a work area.","fact_ids":["sec15-F12","sec15-R03","sec15-F11"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec15-u02-s6","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Regulatory and warning recap","fact_ids":["sec15-F08","sec15-F09","sec15-F10","sec15-R04","sec15-F11","sec15-F12","sec15-R03","sec15-F13"]},"lines":[{"text":"Rectangles: rules, violations to disobey.","fact_ids":["sec15-F08","sec15-F09","sec15-F10","sec15-R04","sec15-F11","sec15-F12","sec15-R03","sec15-F13"]},{"text":"Pennant: no passing starts.","fact_ids":["sec15-F08","sec15-F09","sec15-F10","sec15-R04","sec15-F11","sec15-F12","sec15-R03","sec15-F13"]},{"text":"Diamonds warn; orange means work.","fact_ids":["sec15-F08","sec15-F09","sec15-F10","sec15-R04","sec15-F11","sec15-F12","sec15-R03","sec15-F13"]}],"narration":{"text":"To wrap up, rectangular and square regulatory signs show speed limits and rules such as NO U-TURN, and disobeying them is a traffic violation. A handicap parking sign reserves the space for qualifying people with a handicap plate or placard. The yellow pennant on the left marks the start of a no-passing zone, reinforcing DO NOT PASS. Diamond signs give warnings, normally black on yellow, while black on orange warns of a construction or maintenance area. STOP AHEAD is placed well before a stop sign whose view is blocked. Next, railroad and school signs.","fact_ids":["sec15-F08","sec15-F09","sec15-F10","sec15-R04","sec15-F11","sec15-F12","sec15-R03","sec15-F13"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec15-u03","module_id":"sec15-m03","objective_ids":["sec15-u03"],"title":{"text":"Railroad and school signs","fact_ids":["sec15-F14","sec15-F15","sec15-R05"]},"why_how":[{"text":"The handbook gives railroad crossings an advance sign and a sign at the tracks, plus rules for stopping and looking.","fact_ids":["sec15-F14","sec15-F15","sec15-F16","sec15-F17"]},{"text":"The school sign has its own five-sided shape.","fact_ids":["sec15-F18","sec15-R06"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Quinn is stopped at a railroad crossing with the gate down; the train has passed, but the gate has not yet risen.","fact_ids":["sec15-F16"]},"reasoning":{"text":"Once stopped for a train signal, gate or flagger, stay stopped until the gate rises or the signal or flagger shows it is safe.","fact_ids":["sec15-F16"]},"result":{"text":"Quinn stays stopped until the gate rises.","fact_ids":["sec15-F16","sec15-F27"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: moving as soon as the train passes, before the gate rises.","fact_ids":["sec15-F16"]},"correction":{"text":"Stay stopped until the gate rises or the signal or flagger shows it is safe.","fact_ids":["sec15-F16","sec15-F17"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Wait for the gate.","fact_ids":["sec15-F16"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"Quinn's train has passed, but the crossing gate is still down. May Quinn go?","fact_ids":["sec15-F16"]},"answer":{"text":"No; Quinn stays stopped until the gate rises or it is shown safe.","fact_ids":["sec15-F16"]},"rationale":{"text":"The rule is to stay stopped until the gate rises or the signal or flagger shows it is safe.","fact_ids":["sec15-F16","sec15-F17"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec15-u03-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Rails and schools","fact_ids":["sec15-F14","sec15-F15","sec15-F18"]},"lines":[{"text":"The round RR sign.","fact_ids":["sec15-F14","sec15-F15","sec15-F18"]},{"text":"The crossbuck.","fact_ids":["sec15-F14","sec15-F15","sec15-F18"]},{"text":"The school pentagon.","fact_ids":["sec15-F14","sec15-F15","sec15-F18"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson covers railroad and school signs. You will review the round yellow railroad warning sign, the crossbuck at the tracks, how long to stay stopped for a train signal, gate or flagger, how to look before crossing, the DO NOT STOP ON TRACKS sign, the five-sided school sign, and what happens to speed limits in many school zones. Two contrasts come up often on practice questions: the advance railroad sign versus the crossbuck, and the school pentagon versus the other sign shapes you have learned. Keep each shape tied to where it appears and what it asks of you.","fact_ids":["sec15-F14","sec15-F15","sec15-F18"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec15-u03-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Advance sign and crossbuck","fact_ids":["sec15-F14","sec15-F15"]},"lines":[{"text":"Round yellow sign, black X, RR.","fact_ids":["sec15-F14","sec15-F15"]},{"text":"Slow down; stop if needed.","fact_ids":["sec15-F14","sec15-F15"]},{"text":"Crossbuck: RAILROAD CROSSING.","fact_ids":["sec15-F14","sec15-F15"]}],"narration":{"text":"A round yellow sign with a black X and the letters RR warns of a railroad crossing ahead, so slow down and stop if needed to cross safely. The crossbuck at the tracks reads RAILROAD CROSSING in black on white crosspieces. So there are two railroad signs at two places. The round yellow sign comes first, giving you advance warning while there is still time to slow down. The crossbuck stands at the tracks themselves, marking the crossing. When you see the round sign, begin slowing, and be ready to stop if needed to cross safely.","fact_ids":["sec15-F14","sec15-F15"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec15-u03-s3","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Before or at the crossing","fact_ids":["sec15-R05","sec15-F14","sec15-F15"]},"lines":[{"text":"Round RR sign: advance warning.","fact_ids":["sec15-R05","sec15-F14","sec15-F15"]},{"text":"Crossbuck: at the crossing.","fact_ids":["sec15-R05","sec15-F14","sec15-F15"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. The round yellow RR sign gives advance warning before the crossing, while the white crossbuck stands at the crossing itself. Practice questions may describe the crossbuck as the advance warning, or place the round sign at the tracks. Both reverse the handbook. Think of the order you meet them. First comes the round yellow sign with the black X and the letters RR, telling you a railroad crossing is ahead. Then, at the tracks, comes the crossbuck reading RAILROAD CROSSING in black on white crosspieces. Round before, crossbuck at.","fact_ids":["sec15-R05","sec15-F14","sec15-F15"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec15-u03-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Stopping and looking","fact_ids":["sec15-F16","sec15-F17","sec15-F27"]},"lines":[{"text":"Stay stopped until the gate rises.","fact_ids":["sec15-F16","sec15-F17","sec15-F27"]},{"text":"Look twice in each direction.","fact_ids":["sec15-F16","sec15-F17","sec15-F27"]},{"text":"Never stop on a track.","fact_ids":["sec15-F16","sec15-F17","sec15-F27"]}],"narration":{"text":"Once stopped for a train signal, gate or flagger, stay stopped until the gate rises or the signal or flagger shows it is safe. Before crossing railroad tracks, look twice in each direction. The DO NOT STOP ON TRACKS sign reminds drivers never to stop on a railroad track for any reason. So there are three rules here. When a signal, gate or flagger stops you, the signal, gate or flagger also tells you when to go. Before you cross, look twice each way. And whatever happens, never stop on the track itself, for any reason.","fact_ids":["sec15-F16","sec15-F17","sec15-F27"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec15-u03-s5","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"The school pentagon","fact_ids":["sec15-F18","sec15-F19"]},"lines":[{"text":"Five sides: school zone or crossing.","fact_ids":["sec15-F18","sec15-F19"]},{"text":"Watch especially for children.","fact_ids":["sec15-F18","sec15-F19"]},{"text":"Lower speed during certain hours.","fact_ids":["sec15-F18","sec15-F19"]}],"narration":{"text":"The five-sided pentagon sign warns of a school zone or school crossing, where you should watch especially for children. In many school zones the speed limit is lowered during certain school hours. So the pentagon tells you two things to expect: children who may be crossing or nearby, and in many zones, a lower speed limit during certain school hours. When you see the five-sided sign, watch especially for children and check whether a lower school-zone speed limit applies.
